# Golden bundles

Six real collections from six real Linux userlands — glibc and musl, dpkg and
rpm, systemd and OpenRC — recorded once and committed, and re-evaluated by
`TestGolden` on every `make verify`.

```
                         PASS  FAIL   N/A  UNK   posture   coverage
ubuntu-2404-stock          35    12    32    0      79.3      100
debian-13-stock            34    12    33    0      78.9      100
fedora-44-stock            33    12    33    1      77.8     97.8
rocky-9-stock              33    11    34    1      80.0     97.8
alpine-320-stock           27     7    45    0      84.0      100
ubuntu-2404-hardened       74     4     0    1      96.6     98.7
```

Each `.plb` has a `.expected.json` beside it holding the per-check verdicts, and
a `recipes/<name>.dockerfile` describing exactly what it was recorded from.

## Why these exist

The fixture corpus under `testdata/fixtures/` answers *does this check reach the
right verdict on a tree built to provoke it*. Golden bundles answer a different
question: *did anything move on a host nobody was thinking about when the change
was written*. Only the second one catches a check whose blast radius is wider
than its author believed, because a fixture is written by the same person, at
the same time, with the same misconception.

`ubuntu-2404-hardened` is the one that carries the catalog. Every check in the
catalog reaches a real verdict on it — no `NOT_APPLICABLE` at all — which no
fixture and no stock image manages alone.

## Working with them

```
make golden-diff       # read-only: which bundles no longer match, and where
make golden-update     # rewrite the .expected.json files, then read the diff
testdata/bundles/record.sh [name...]   # re-record the bundles themselves
```

`record.sh` needs docker. Nothing in CI runs it, and `make verify` never does:
re-recording is a deliberate act with a reviewed diff, not a build step.

Two gates guard the corpus and they are deliberately different in kind. The
`.expected.json` files hold per-check verdicts and are regenerated by
`make golden-update`; the counts and posture in `internal/cli/golden_test.go`
are typed by hand. The second exists because the first is too easy to satisfy —
`-update` makes any diff go away, and a gate that can be silenced by the same
command that runs it will eventually be silenced by habit.

**Changing a hand-typed number is the moment somebody claims a new verdict is
correct.** Not when the check changed, and not when `-update` ran.

## What is in them, and what is not

Recorded with `--redact`, so no hostname was ever written to disk. Passed
through `tools/goldenrecord`, which removes what a containerised recording
leaks through the kernel mount table: the runtime's overlay directories and the
per-container bind paths behind `/etc/hostname`, `/etc/hosts` and
`/etc/resolv.conf`. Every substitution it makes is printed when it runs.

Every committed bundle has an empty `meta`, and that is a fossil rather than a
choice: they were recorded before WP-37, when `/etc/os-release` being a symlink
on every systemd distribution meant the read silently failed. `--redact` drops
the hostname regardless; the next re-recording will pick up `os_release`. No
check reads `meta`, so no expectation depends on it.

Timestamps, `bundle_id` and `tool.version` are left alone. They are the
provenance of the recording and they name a commit in this repository, not a
person; normalising them would make the artifact prettier and less true.

`ubuntu-2404-hardened` is recorded from a host with a real login account,
because `USERS-0004`, `USERS-0009` and `USERS-0010` ask about accounts that can
actually authenticate and no stock image has one. No credential reaches the
bundle: `/etc/shadow` is never stored as evidence, and the shadow fact records
only the *properties* of a hash — which algorithm, locked, empty — never the
hash. `TestGoldenBundlesCarryNoCredentialMaterial` is that design decision's
alarm, and `TestGoldenBundlesCarryNothingOfTheRecordingHost` is the redaction
gate. Both read the raw archive rather than the decoded facts, because the
failure being guarded against is a value arriving somewhere nobody thought to
look.

Every bundle contains `/usr/local/bin/plumbline` in its filesystem facts. That
is not contamination to apologise for: it is what every real scan sees, because
a host being audited has the auditor installed on it.

## What a container cannot be

Two of the four `ubuntu-2404-hardened` failures are `/tmp` and `/home` not being
separate mounts, and two are kernel parameters that cannot be set because
`/proc/sys` is read-only without `--privileged`. They are correct `FAIL`s — the
recorded host genuinely is in that state — and a recipe that ran `--privileged`
to make the number prettier would be recording a host nobody has.

## The three UNKNOWNs

They are the most valuable findings in the corpus, because they are the ones
another scanner would report as a `PASS`.

`ubuntu-2404-hardened` carries `KERNEL-0007`. Ubuntu ships
`/etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf` as a symlink, the live seam opens privileged
reads with `O_NOFOLLOW` and so declines to follow it, and the check will not
claim the running kernel matches its configuration when one of the configuration
files was not among the ones it read.

`fedora-44-stock` and `rocky-9-stock` both carry `AUTH-0002`. Both enforce
`pam_pwquality` and then set none of its parameters, so the effective minimum
password length comes from libpwquality's compiled-in default — a property of a
binary, not of any file on the host. The check says it does not know. Reporting
the documented default here would be inventing a fact about a host from a
manual page.

## Six

`docs/ROADMAP.md` sets a v1.0.0 release criterion of golden bundles for **six**
distribution/version combinations. These are those six, and the count was met by
covering families rather than by counting: glibc and musl, dpkg and rpm, systemd
and OpenRC, Fedora's leading edge and a conservative RHEL rebuild, and one host
configured the way somebody would actually want it.

Adding a seventh is worth doing when it covers something none of these do — a
distribution with a different init, a different PAM generator, a different
default umask. Adding Ubuntu 22.04 beside 24.04 would grow the corpus without
growing what it can catch.
